title: Learning styles: a popular claim that fails its own test

blocks.html: Checked against the sources as they stood on 2026-09-25.

blocks.label: Definition
blocks.html:
“Learning styles” is the idea that people differ in which mode of teaching or study works best for them.

Pashler, McDaniel, Rohrer and Bjork (2008) keep two claims apart. The first is that people will state preferences about how they like to take in new material. The second, the learning-styles hypothesis, is that teaching fitted to a learner’s style gives a better learning outcome. Its commonest version is the meshing hypothesis: teaching works best in the format that matches the learner’s preference, pictures for a “visual learner”, say.

They set four conditions an experiment must meet before it supports the hypothesis. Learners are divided into two or more groups by a measure of style. Within each group, they are allocated at random to one of two or more teaching methods. Everyone takes the same test; if the tests differ, no support is possible. And the method that gives one group its best test score is not the method that gives another group its best. They call that last pattern a crossover interaction, drawn with the style groups along the bottom axis of a graph.

With two styles and two methods, the mean scores make a 2 × 2 table, read “two by two”: two rows and two columns. Each row is a style group and each column a method. Within one row, the two cells are two groups allocated at random, so the difference between their means is the mean difference (MD), as in section 2. Take the MD the same way round in both rows, say the first method minus the second. A crossover is present when one row’s MD is positive and the other’s is negative. The best column then differs from row to row.

A crossover can be present even when one style group scores higher than the other on both methods. Pashler’s criterion does not ask that each group’s best method be its matched one. Meshing asks that as well. Pashler calls the version without that demand the broad version of the hypothesis: the best method differs between style groups, whichever way round. So a crossover the wrong way round, each group best with the method that does not match its label, supports the broad version and contradicts meshing.

When both MDs have the same sign, the same method is best for every learner, and the result is no evidence for learning styles, however different the two MDs are in size. Read down the columns instead of across the rows, and such a result can look like a crossover.

Studies with the right design found no support, one of them with 123 internal medicine residents. Pashler and colleagues conclude that applying learning styles in classrooms is unwarranted.

blocks.label: In plain terms
blocks.html:
The claim goes like this: some people learn best from pictures, some from words, some by doing, so find out which kind each learner is and teach each one their way. Here is the test it has to pass.

Take learners of two styles. Split each group in two by lottery, and teach one half one way and the other half the other way. Test everyone the same way. The best method has to change from one group to the other. That change is the crossover.

Notice what does not count. Pictures working better for everyone does not count, even if they help visual learners more. Visual learners scoring higher than verbal learners does not count either.

blocks.alt: Grouped bars for two style groups. For the visual group the diagram bar, 70, is taller than the text bar, 60. For the verbal group the text bar, 67, is taller than the diagram bar, 58.
blocks.caption: Made-up numbers, not data, drawn with the style groups along the bottom as Pashler’s test asks. Diagrams give the visual group its best score, 70% against 60%, and text gives the verbal group its best, 67% against 58%. The best lesson changes with the group: a crossover.

blocks.alt: Bars for the visual and verbal groups under two made-up tables. First table: a bar of 10 pointing up for the visual group and a bar of -9 pointing down for the verbal group. Second table: bars of 12 and 2, both pointing up.
blocks.caption: Made-up numbers, not data. The MD, diagram minus text, within each group. In the first table the bars point opposite ways, 10 and -9: a crossover. In the second both point up, 12 and 2: diagrams are best for both groups, and there is no crossover.

blocks.alt: Grouped bars for two lessons. Diagram lesson: visual 72, verbal 65. Text lesson: visual 60, verbal 63. The taller bar switches from visual to verbal between the lessons.
blocks.caption: The second made-up table, drawn with the lessons along the bottom instead. Visual beats verbal on diagrams, 72 against 65, and verbal beats visual on text, 63 against 60, so the pattern seems to cross. Read within each group and diagrams are best for both: 72 against 60, and 65 against 63.

blocks.caption: 93% of 137 UK schoolteachers (2012) and 58% of 114 UK academics agreed that people learn better in their preferred style. After being shown that the evidence is missing, 32% said they still planned to account for learning styles in their teaching. The first bar is a different sample from the other two.

blocks.label: Illustration 1
blocks.html:
Open Pashler, McDaniel, Rohrer and Bjork, “Learning styles: concepts and evidence”, Psychological Science in the Public Interest 2008, at https://doi.org/10.1111/j.1539-6053.2009.01038.x. Search for Fourth, the results.

Fourth, the results need to show that the learning method that optimizes test performance of one learning-style group is different than the learning method that optimizes the test performance of a second learning-style group.

That is the whole test. Now put it in a table. The numbers below are made up to show the logic. They come from no study.

Eighty MBBS students fill in a learning-style questionnaire. Forty come out visual and forty verbal. Within each group, a lottery sends half to a lesson on reading a food label taught with diagrams. The other half get the same lesson taught as text. A week later all eighty sit the same test. Here are the mean scores, as a percentage of the maximum.

style group diagram lesson text lesson
visual 70% 60%
verbal 58% 67%

Work across each row, not down each column. The question a teacher faces is which lesson to give this learner, so compare the two lessons within one group. Take the MD, diagram minus text, in percentage points.

visual: 70 minus 60 = 10
verbal: 58 minus 67 = -9

One MD is positive and the other negative. Diagrams are best for the visual group and text is best for the verbal group. The best lesson changes with the group. That is a crossover, and in this made-up table it runs the way meshing predicts.

Now change the bottom row. Same design, different made-up numbers:

style group diagram lesson text lesson
visual 72% 60%
verbal 65% 63%

visual: 72 minus 60 = 12
verbal: 65 minus 63 = 2

Both MDs are positive. Diagrams are best for both groups, so there is no crossover. The difference is bigger for the visual group, but a bigger difference is not a different best lesson. Teach everyone with diagrams.

Now read the second table down its columns, and watch it argue the opposite. On diagrams, visual beats verbal, 72 against 65. On text, verbal beats visual, 63 against 60. “Each group wins on its own method.” Draw it with the lessons along the bottom and the bars seem to cross. Search the review for horizontal axis.

the choice of variable for the horizontal axis can affect whether an interaction appears to “cross over.”

Reading down a column compares two different sets of people, who differ in more than their style. It does not tell you which lesson to give the verbal student in front of you.

blocks.label: Where this picture breaks
blocks.html: Both tables are invented. They show what the test reads, not what any study found. A real table from one study can show a crossover by chance, when both MDs are small beside the spread of the scores. Pashler and colleagues assume every pattern in their figure is statistically significant, which roughly means too large to put down to chance. Telling a real crossover from a chance one needs a statistical test this book does not teach, and a repeat of the study.

blocks.label: Illustration 2
blocks.html:
Now see what happened when researchers looked for the crossover. In the same review, search for only one study.

we found only one study that could be described as even potentially meeting the criteria described earlier

That study, by Sternberg and colleagues (1999), gave an ability test to 324 high school students. Search for 112.

the authors selected a subset of 112 subjects (35%) for whom one of these three abilities was much higher than the other two

Check the share yourself.

112 divided by 324 = 0.345679012

About 35%, as printed. So the reported crossover rests on about a third of the students tested. The reviewers add that it appeared only in heavily processed scores, and only after some students’ scores were dropped for reasons not given. They call it tenuous.

Now search for internal medicine.

Studying a sample of 123 internal medicine residents and presenting modules on four ambulatory medicine topics, they found no support for this prediction.

The prediction was that residents of one style would learn better with the problem shown before the content, and residents of another style with the reverse. This study met the design, on doctors in training, and found no support for the predicted crossover.

One more, whose pattern you can now read. Search for Visual presentations produced.

Visual presentations produced better free recall than did purely verbal presentations

In that study, words shown as line drawings were recalled better than words only heard. A person’s questionnaire score was not related in any clear way to which way suited them. That is close to the same-sign pattern of the second made-up table: one method best for all. Now read the review’s conclusion. Search for unwarranted.

lead us to conclude that any application of learning styles in classrooms is unwarranted

blocks.label: Where this picture breaks
blocks.html: The review is from 2008 and covers what had been published by then. The authors say plainly that the negative results are not a conclusive refutation. Many versions of learning styles have never been tested at all. “No adequate evidence” is the claim the review supports. “Proven false for every version” is not.

blocks.label: Illustration 3
blocks.html:
Open Newton and Miah, “Evidence-based higher education – is the learning styles ‘myth’ important?”, Frontiers in Psychology 2017, at https://www.frontiersin.org/journals/psychology/articles/10.3389/fpsyg.2017.00444/full. They surveyed 114 academics at UK universities. Search for 2012 study.

In a 2012 study, 93% of a sample of 137 UK school teachers agreed with the statement “Individuals learn better when they receive information in their preferred learning style (e.g., auditory, visual, kinesthetic).” In our sample of academics in UK Higher Education, 58% agreed with that same statement

Now search for Thirty-three.

Thirty-three percent of participants reported having used Learning Styles in the last 12 months

Belief ran well ahead of use. The survey then explained the missing evidence, and asked again. Search for 32%.

a substantial number of participants (32%) stated that they would continue to use Learning Styles despite being presented with the lack of an evidence base to support them

So expect the idea in your own staff room. Expect, too, that the evidence alone will not move everyone. The weakness these academics agreed with most was that the theory is conceptually flawed. The authors give an example. Search for heart sounds.

teaching medical students to recognize heart sounds would be impossible using visual methods, whereas teaching them to recognize different skin rashes would be impossible using sounds

The content decides how it must be taught, not a label on the learner. Every student listens to a murmur. Every student looks at a rash. When you teach accredited social health activist (ASHA) workers to measure a waist with a tape, every one of them holds the tape, whatever each says her style is.

blocks.label: Where this picture breaks
blocks.html: The survey is of UK university teachers who chose to answer it; the authors call it a convenience sample. It measures what they believe, not whether learning styles work. None of its figures describe Indian teachers. And “would continue” is a stated plan, not something the survey watched them do.

points.html: “Learners have learning styles, so teaching to them helps” joins two claims. Accept the first; refuse the second.
To test any claim that matching helps, ask for all four cells. Take the MD within each group, the same way round. Only opposite signs make a crossover.
Comparing down a column, visual learners against verbal learners on the same lesson, is not the test. Compare the two lessons within one group.
A lesson that is better for one group by a lot and for the other by a little is still better for both. Teach everyone with it.
Rejecting learning styles is not a vote for teaching everyone one way. Choose methods for the material and the level.
Cook and colleagues, reported by Pashler, split 123 internal medicine residents by style and by method. They found no support for matching.
Expect the idea among colleagues. Lead with the content argument: a murmur has to be heard and a rash has to be seen.
Say “there is no adequate evidence for it”, not “it has been proven false”. A crossover in one small table can also arise by chance: the MD check reads the pattern, not whether it is real.

blocks.prompt: A colleague wants a learning-style questionnaire to decide how your department teaches community medicine to MBBS students. Specify the study that could settle it for two styles, visual and verbal, and two ways of teaching one topic. Say what result would support matching, and what result would not.
blocks.answer:
Classify first. Every student in the batch takes the questionnaire. Keep the two style groups, visual and verbal, and write down beforehand how a student is placed in each.

Allocate within each group. A lottery sends half of each style group to method one, say a session built on diagrams. The other half get method two, the same content as written text. Same teacher, same time, same content.

Test everyone the same way. One test, written before the teaching, taken by all students after the same delay, a week or more (section 2). If the groups sit different tests, nothing can be concluded about styles.

Read the result across the rows. Take the MD, diagrams minus text, within each style group. Support for matching needs opposite signs, with each group best on its own matched method. The same sign in both groups means one method is best for everyone, however different the two MDs. A group that scores higher on both methods tells you nothing either way.

Say what a single result is worth. One batch can show a crossover by chance. Ask for a statistical test of the crossover and a repeat in another batch before any student is sorted.

blocks.prompt: A 2 × 2 table has rows P and Q and columns X and Y. Row P: X = 60, Y = 70. Row Q: X = 50, Y = 65. In each row, which column is higher? Is there a crossover?
blocks.answer:
Compare the two columns within each row.

row P: 70 is higher than 60, so Y
row Q: 65 is higher than 50, so Y

Both rows are highest in column Y. The best column does not change from row to row, so there is no crossover.

blocks.prompt: Row P: X = 72, Y = 64. Row Q: X = 58, Y = 66. Work out X minus Y in each row, and say whether there is a crossover.
blocks.answer:
Subtract within each row, the same way round.

row P: 72 minus 64 = 8
row Q: 58 minus 66 = -8

One difference is positive and the other negative. X is best in row P and Y is best in row Q. There is a crossover.

blocks.prompt: Row P: X = 55, and X minus Y = -6. Row Q: Y = 66, and X minus Y = 4. Find the missing Y in row P and the missing X in row Q. Is there a crossover?
blocks.answer:
In row P, X minus Y = -6, so Y is 6 more than X.

Y = 55 plus 6 = 61
check: 55 minus 61 = -6

In row Q, X minus Y = 4, so X is 4 more than Y.

X = 66 plus 4 = 70
check: 70 minus 66 = 4

Row P is best in Y (61 against 55). Row Q is best in X (70 against 66). The signs are opposite, so there is a crossover.

blocks.prompt:
Made-up numbers, from no study. Sixty MBBS students take a learning-style questionnaire. Within each style group, a lottery sends half to a lesson on reading a food label taught with diagrams. The other half get the same lesson as text. A week later all of them take the same test.

Mean scores: visual group, diagram 80%, text 72%. Verbal group, diagram 55%, text 63%. A colleague says: “The verbal group did worse on both lessons, so this tells us nothing about matching.” Is there a crossover, and is the colleague right?
blocks.answer:
Take the MD, diagram minus text, within each group, in percentage points.

visual: 80 minus 72 = 8
verbal: 55 minus 63 = -8

The signs are opposite, so there is a crossover. Diagrams are best for the visual group and text for the verbal group: each group’s best lesson is its matched one. In this made-up table, the pattern is the one meshing predicts.

The colleague is wrong. That one group scores lower on both lessons is a difference between the groups. The test asks something else: within each group, which lesson is better? A crossover can be present even when one group outscores the other on every method.

blocks.prompt: Made-up numbers, from no study. The same design as before. Visual group: diagram 75%, text 60%. Verbal group: diagram 64%, text 62%. Is there a crossover, and what should the teacher do?
blocks.answer:
MD, diagram minus text, within each group, in percentage points.

visual: 75 minus 60 = 15
verbal: 64 minus 62 = 2

Both MDs are positive. Diagrams are best for both groups, by 15 points for the visual group and 2 points for the verbal group. The two MDs differ in size, not in sign, so there is no crossover. Meshing would send the verbal students to the text lesson, and on these numbers they do slightly worse there. Teach everyone with diagrams. A 2-point difference may also be chance; the table alone cannot say.

blocks.prompt:
Made-up numbers, from no study. Forty ASHA workers answer a questionnaire that labels them visual or auditory. Within each group, a lottery sends half to a session on the child growth chart taught with picture cards. The other half get the same session as a spoken explanation. Everyone takes the same test a week later.

Visual group: picture cards 58%, spoken 66%. Auditory group: picture cards 71%, spoken 63%. Is there a crossover? Does it support learning styles, and does it support meshing?
blocks.answer:
MD, picture cards minus spoken, within each group, in percentage points.

visual: 58 minus 66 = -8
auditory: 71 minus 63 = 8

The signs are opposite, so there is a crossover: the best session changes with the group. But look at which session wins. The visual group does best with the spoken session, and the auditory group with the picture cards. Each group does best with the method that does not match its label.

Suppose a result like this were real and repeated. It would support Pashler’s broad version of learning styles: sorting by the questionnaire would tell you which session to give. It contradicts meshing, because matching the session to the label would give each group its worse session.

blocks.prompt:
Here is a worked answer. Find the step that broke. Made-up numbers: visual group, diagram 68%, text 57%; verbal group, diagram 62%, text 59%.

on diagrams, visual 68 beats verbal 62
on text, verbal 59 beats visual 57
each group wins on its own method
so there is a crossover, and matching works
blocks.answer:
The first two lines broke it. Each compares the two style groups on one lesson: down a column. The test compares the two lessons within one group: across a row.

visual: 68 minus 57 = 11
verbal: 62 minus 59 = 3

Both MDs are positive. Diagrams are best for both groups, so there is no crossover. The verbal students do better with diagrams too.

Why the wrong answer looks reasonable. It does find each group “winning” on its own method, and drawn with the lessons along the bottom the bars do seem to cross. Pashler and colleagues warn of exactly this. But the winning is against a different set of people. A teacher choosing a lesson for a verbal student compares that student’s two options, and on these numbers diagrams win.

blocks.prompt:
Here is a worked answer. Find the step that broke. Made-up numbers.

visual learners taught with diagrams: mean 71%
verbal learners taught with text: mean 69%
both matched groups scored well above the 50% pass mark
so matching teaching to style works
blocks.answer:
The last step broke, and it broke because the table is half empty. Only two of the four cells are there: the two matched ones. There is no score for visual learners taught with text, and none for verbal learners taught with diagrams. So no MD can be taken within either group, and no crossover can be looked for.

The comparison the worked answer does make is against a pass mark. That shows both groups passed. It says nothing about whether either group would have done better or worse with the other lesson. If visual learners taught with text had also scored 71%, matching would have made no difference at all.

Why the wrong answer looks reasonable. Both numbers are high, and each group got the lesson that matched its style. Success under matching feels like evidence for matching. It is only evidence when the unmatched cells are there to compare with.

blocks.prompt: A colleague says in a department meeting: “We tried it. The visual learners in our batch scored 74% after the diagram session, and the whole batch averaged 66% after the text session. So visual learners do better when we teach visually.” Decide what to compute, compute it, and say what your answer does not establish.
blocks.answer:
What to compute: the only difference the numbers allow, and then which cells of the 2 × 2 table it fills.

74 minus 66 = 8

8 percentage points. But this is not an MD within any group. It sets one subgroup under one session against the whole batch under another session. The whole batch includes the visual learners themselves, and everyone else.

What it does not establish. It does not show that visual learners do better with diagrams than with text, because their own text score is not given. It does not show a crossover, because there is no verbal group, and no cell for either group under the other session. The two sessions may also have differed in content, in test, or in time of year, and nobody was allocated to a session by lottery. What to ask for: both style groups, each split at random between the two sessions, and the same test for all.

blocks.prompt: A senior teacher says in a curriculum committee: “Most teachers believe in learning styles. Newton and Miah found 58% of 114 UK academics agreed, and an earlier study found 93% of 137 schoolteachers agreed. That many people cannot all be wrong.” Decide what to compute, compute it, and say what your answer does not establish.
blocks.answer:
What to compute: how many people the percentages stand for, so the claim is sized.

0.58 times 114 = 66.12
0.93 times 137 = 127.41

About 66 academics and about 127 schoolteachers. The percentages are rounded, so the counts are approximate.

The premise is true: these surveys did find those levels of agreement. The inference does not carry (Book 0, F4). A survey of belief measures what people think works. Whether matching teaching to style improves learning is a different question, and the crossover test answers it. Pashler and colleagues found one doubtful study that even potentially met the test. The studies that met it properly, one of them with 123 internal medicine residents, found no support.

What this does not establish. It does not establish that learning styles are proven useless in every version: the same review says many versions have never been tested. It does not tell you what teachers in India believe, because neither survey asked them. And the 66 and 127 are counts of people agreeing with a sentence, not of people shown to teach better by it.
